headline: Afghan Midwives Transform Maternal Care in Remote Villages
meta_description: Over 450 community health houses run by Afghan midwives are saving mothers' and babies' lives in remote areas where hospital access is nearly impossible.
summary_short: Afghan midwives at remote clinics are providing life-saving prenatal care and emergency delivery services to thousands of women in villages hours from hospitals.
body:
In the remote villages of Afghanistan, where two-thirds of women have no access to health care, a network of 450 community clinics is quietly saving lives. At the Arkalik family health house in Farhan province, midwife Laila Amini has not recorded a single pregnancy-related death in seven years—a remarkable achievement in a country considered one of the most dangerous places in the world to be a mother. These clinics, called Ashiana-e-Sehi in the local Dari language and supported by the UN Population Fund since 2009, bring trained midwives within walking distance of women who might otherwise travel 80 miles on treacherous mountain roads to reach a hospital.

Ram Bibi, a 30-year-old mother in Helmand province, represents the difference these clinics make. Her first five children were born at home without skilled assistance, leaving both mother and newborns vulnerable to infection. Now pregnant with her sixth child, she receives regular prenatal checkups, anemia screening, and vaccinations at her nearby family health house. When midwife Marzia screened another patient, Manawara, she detected a dangerous breech position at 38 weeks of pregnancy—a complication that likely would have been fatal without immediate intervention.

The model works because it meets women where they are. An assessment across six provinces found that 88.7 percent of women rated their local family health house as "very important" for reproductive and maternal health. Nearly three-quarters of women surveyed lived within one kilometer of their clinic, and 82 percent could walk to it. Yet challenges remain severe. Midwives at some clinics see 20 to 60 patients daily—far exceeding capacity—and the December 2024 ban on women's medical education threatens future training. Digital learning through apps in Dari and Pashto has become the lifeline for ongoing midwife education. Despite these obstacles, these clinics represent an essential lifeline in a collapsing health system.
quick_facts: 450 UN-supported community clinics serve remote Afghan villages since 2009
Arkalik clinic: zero pregnancy-related deaths recorded in seven years
82% of surveyed women can walk to their nearest family health house
Midwives see up to 70 patients daily, despite clinics designed for 300 monthly
